title: Library Imports
content: Imports Mathlib's inner product space (providing `dist` on $\mathbb{R}^2$), Finset cardinality, real number basics, and general tactics for the formalization of planar point configurations.
mathContext: The `dist` function from `Analysis.InnerProductSpace.Basic` gives Euclidean distance on $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$. `Finset.Card` provides the cardinality function used to count distinct distances.

title: Point Configuration
content: An $n$-point configuration in $\mathbb{R}^2$, defined as a function $\text{Fin}\;n \to \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$. Points are indexed by finite type for decidable enumeration.
mathContext: Using $\text{Fin}\;n \to \mathbb{R}^2$ allows Finset operations over the index set. The configuration is not required to have distinct points unless additional hypotheses are imposed.

title: No Four Concyclic
content: No four points lie on a common circle: for all distinct $i_1, i_2, i_3, i_4$, there is no circle (center $c$, radius $r > 0$) passing through all four. This is the key geometric restriction of Problem #654.
mathContext: A circle in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is determined by 3 non-collinear points. The no-four-concyclic condition means every circle passes through at most 3 configuration points. Since points at distance $d$ from $x_i$ lie on a circle of radius $d$ centered at $x_i$, at most 3 points share any distance from $x_i$ — this is the source of the $(n-1)/3$ bound.

title: Distinct Distances from a Point
content: Counts $|\{\mathrm{dist}(x_i, x_j) : j \ne i\}|$, the number of distinct distance values from point $x_i$ to all other configuration points. Defined noncomputably via Finset image cardinality.
mathContext: This is the per-point distinct distance count $D(x_i) = |\{d(x_i, x_j) : j \ne i\}|$. The Erdős distinct distances conjecture (resolved by Guth-Katz for all pairs) asks about $\sum_i D(x_i)$; Problem #654 asks about $\max_i D(x_i)$ under geometric restrictions.

title: Maximum Distinct Distances
content: The supremum of `distinctDistances P i` over all points $i$ in the configuration. Uses `Finset.sup'` with a default witness at index 0.
mathContext: This captures $\max_{1 \le i \le n} D(x_i)$. The conjecture asserts this maximum is $(1 - o(1))n$, meaning for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and large enough $n$, $\max_i D(x_i) \ge (1 - \varepsilon)n$.

title: Known Lower Bound $(n-1)/3$
content: Every point has at least $(n-1)/3$ distinct distances under the no-four-concyclic condition. Proof: the circle of radius $d$ centered at $x_i$ contains at most 3 configuration points (including $x_i$), so at most 3 points share each distance, giving $\ge (n-1)/3$ distinct values.
mathContext: This is a pigeonhole argument: $n-1$ other points, each distance repeated at most 3 times (by the concyclic bound), yields $\ge (n-1)/3$ distinct distances. The factor 3 comes from the circle through $x_i$ containing at most 3 other points — but actually at most 2, since $x_i$ is the center, not on the circle. The bound may be improvable to $(n-1)/2$.

title: Main Conjecture (Axiomatized)
content: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ and sufficiently large $n$, any $n$-point configuration with no four concyclic has some point with $\ge (1 - \varepsilon)n$ distinct distances. The conjecture is stated with explicit $\varepsilon$-$N$ quantifiers, formalizing the $o(1)$ error.
mathContext: The statement $\forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists N,\; \forall n \ge N,\; \forall P,\; \text{NoFourConcyclic}(P) \implies \exists i,\; (1-\varepsilon)n \le D(x_i)$ is the formal version of 'some point has $(1-o(1))n$ distinct distances'. The gap between the known $(n-1)/3 \approx 0.33n$ and the conjectured $(1-o(1))n$ is enormous.

title: No Three Collinear (General Position)
content: No three points are collinear: for distinct $i_1, i_2, i_3$, there is no line $ax + by = c$ (with $(a,b) \ne (0,0)$) containing all three. This is a weaker restriction than no-four-concyclic.
mathContext: General position (no three collinear) is the standard non-degeneracy assumption in discrete geometry. It is strictly weaker than no-four-concyclic: collinear points lie on a 'circle of infinite radius', so no-four-concyclic implies no-four-collinear but not vice versa. The Erdős-Pach variant uses this weaker condition.

title: Erdős-Pach Weaker Variant (Axiomatized)
content: Under general position (no three collinear), does some point have $\ge (1/3 + c)n$ distinct distances for an absolute constant $c > 0$? This is weaker than the main conjecture but still open.
mathContext: Erdős and Pach posed this in 1990 as a stepping stone. Without any restriction, the Szemerédi-Trotter incidence bound gives $\Omega(n^{4/5})$ distinct distances from some point. The $1/3$ baseline comes from the trivial pigeonhole bound under no-three-collinear (at most 2 points share each distance from a given point via a line). Improving beyond $1/3$ requires new geometric arguments.

title: Guth-Katz Distinct Distances Context
content: The Guth-Katz theorem (2015) gives $\Omega(n / \log n)$ total distinct distances for any $n$-point configuration, without geometric restrictions. This resolves the Erdős distinct distances conjecture up to the log factor.
mathContext: Guth and Katz proved that $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ determine $\Omega(n / \log n)$ distinct distances, using algebraic geometry (polynomial partitioning) and the Elekes-Sharir framework reducing distances to line intersections in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Problem #654 is complementary: it asks for near-$n$ from a **single** point but requires the no-four-concyclic condition. The two results use very different techniques.

title: Circle Distance Bound
content: Under no-four-concyclic, at most 3 points (besides $x_i$) share any given distance $d > 0$ from $x_i$. These points lie on the circle of radius $d$ centered at $x_i$, which meets at most 3 other configuration points.
mathContext: The set $\{j \ne i : d(x_i, x_j) = d\}$ lies on a circle centered at $x_i$ with radius $d$. Including $x_i$, this circle passes through at most 3 + 1 = 4 configuration points — but wait, $x_i$ is the center, not on the circle. So the circle passes through at most 3 points (from no-four-concyclic applied to any 4 of them plus the degenerate case). The bound of 3 is sharp.
